      Single dental implant (post, abutment, and crown)
      £2,000 – £3,500
    
    
      Implant-supported bridge (multiple teeth)
      £4,000 – £8,000+
    
    
      Full arch implant restoration
      £8,000 – £20,000+
    
    
      Bone grafting (if required)
      £400 – £1,500+
    
  
  These are approximate ranges based on typical London private practice pricing and are not quotes. Your individual cost will depend on your clinical assessment.


For patients replacing multiple teeth, implant-supported bridges or full-arch restorations may be discussed. These involve fewer implants than replacing each tooth individually, but the restorative work is more complex, which is reflected in the cost.

Transparent pricing matters. When comparing quotes, it is important to check whether the figure includes all components — the implant, the abutment, the crown, and any follow-up appointments — or whether these are itemised separately.


Factors That Influence Implant Cost

Not every implant case is the same, and several factors can cause the cost of treatment to vary from one patient to another:


  Complexity of the case — straightforward single-tooth replacements tend to be less costly than cases involving multiple missing teeth, compromised bone, or other clinical challenges.
  Bone grafting or ridge augmentation — if there is insufficient bone volume at the implant site, a grafting procedure may be needed before or alongside implant placement. This adds both clinical time and material costs.
  Implant brand and materials — implant systems vary in quality, documentation, and long-term evidence. Well-established implant brands with proven track records may carry higher costs, but they also offer greater confidence in component availability and clinical support.
  Crown material and laboratory work — the final restoration is custom-made in a dental laboratory. The choice of material (such as porcelain or zirconia) and the quality of the laboratory work influence the overall cost.
  Number of implants required — replacing several teeth or a full arch requires more clinical planning, surgical time, and restorative work.
  Preparatory treatments — some patients may need tooth extractions, gum treatment, or other preparatory procedures before implants can be placed.


These variables are precisely why a personalised assessment is important. A headline price cannot account for the clinical specifics of your situation.


Additional Costs to Consider

Beyond the implant procedure itself, there are a few additional costs worth factoring into your budget:


  Initial consultation — most private clinics charge a fee for the assessment appointment, during which your dentist will examine your mouth, discuss your options, and begin planning treatment.
  X-rays and diagnostic records — basic imaging is usually needed to assess bone levels and plan implant positioning. These may be included in the consultation fee or charged separately.
  Follow-up appointments — implant treatment typically involves several review visits during the healing period and after the final crown is fitted. Check whether these are included in the overall fee.
  Ongoing maintenance — once the implant is in place, regular hygiene appointments and dental check-ups are an important part of long-term care. These are an ongoing cost to factor in.


When reviewing a quote, it is reasonable to ask what is included and what might be billed separately. A good practice will be transparent about this from the outset.


Is the Most Expensive Option Always Better?

Not necessarily — but very low prices should prompt questions, just as very high ones should. Cost can reflect clinical quality, but it can also reflect overheads, location, or marketing spend. What matters most is what is included, how the treatment is planned, and whether the implant system and materials are well-documented and reliable.

Rather than choosing based on price alone, it can be more useful to focus on:


  Whether the treatment plan is based on a thorough clinical assessment
  The implant brand being used and its clinical track record
  The quality and source of the laboratory work
  Whether follow-up care is part of the package
  The transparency and detail of the quote


Implant treatment is a long-term investment in your oral health. Understanding what you are paying for — and why — is more valuable than simply finding the lowest number.


Payment Options and Budget Planning

Dental implants represent a significant financial commitment, and many patients understandably want to explore ways to manage the cost. Several options may be available depending on the practice:


  Interest-free finance — some practices offer 0% finance plans that allow you to spread the cost of treatment over several months, making it more manageable on a monthly basis. Eligibility is usually subject to a credit check.
  Phased treatment — because implant treatment takes place over several stages (surgery, healing, crown fitting), payments can sometimes be spread across these phases rather than paid as a lump sum.
  Membership plans — some practices offer membership plans that provide discounted rates on treatments, including implants. These can offer meaningful savings, particularly for patients planning multiple procedures.


When budgeting, it helps to have a clear understanding of the total cost upfront, including any additional procedures that may be needed. Ask your practice for a written treatment plan with an itemised breakdown before committing.


How to Get an Accurate Quote

The only reliable way to get an accurate cost for dental implant treatment is through a clinical consultation. During this appointment, your dentist will:


  Examine your mouth and assess the area where the implant is needed
  Evaluate your bone levels and gum health
  Discuss your medical history and any factors that may influence treatment
  Explain the proposed treatment plan, including any preparatory work
  Provide a detailed, written cost estimate


It is a good idea to come to your consultation with questions prepared. You might want to ask:


  What implant system is being used, and why?
  Is the quoted price inclusive of all stages, or are some elements billed separately?
  What happens if additional treatment is needed during the process?
  Are follow-up appointments included?
  What finance or payment options are available?


A thorough consultation should leave you feeling informed and confident about both the clinical plan and the financial commitment involved.


Booking a Cost Consultation in London

If you are considering dental implants and want to understand the costs involved, the first step is to book a consultation. This gives you the opportunity to have your mouth assessed, discuss your goals, and receive a personalised treatment plan with clear pricing.

At our London practice, we aim to be upfront about costs from the start. We provide written treatment plans that outline every element of the proposed work, so you know exactly what is included. We also offer transparent fee information and are happy to discuss finance options to help make treatment more accessible.

Bring a list of any questions you have — about cost, treatment stages, timelines, or aftercare. An honest conversation about pricing is an important part of the process, and it is something we actively encourage.

Frequently Asked Questions


  
    How much do dental implants cost in London?

acceptedAnswer.text: In London, a single dental implant (including the post, abutment, and crown) typically costs between £2,000 and £3,500, depending on the complexity of the case, the materials used, and any additional procedures required. Actual costs can only be confirmed following a clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Why do implant costs vary so much?

acceptedAnswer.text: Costs vary because each case is different. Factors such as bone quality, the need for grafting, the number of teeth being replaced, the implant system used, and the type of crown material all influence the final price. Location and practice overheads also play a role.

Most standard dental insurance plans in the UK do not cover dental implants, as they are considered a private treatment. However, some higher-level plans may contribute towards certain elements. It is worth checking with your provider to see if any coverage applies to your plan.

mainEntity.name: Are implant costs the same everywhere in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Costs tend to be higher in London and other major cities due to higher overheads and operating costs. Practices outside London may offer lower prices, though quality and included services should always be compared carefully.

mainEntity.name: What additional costs might be involved?

acceptedAnswer.text: Depending on your case, additional costs may include the initial consultation, X-rays, bone grafting, tooth extractions, and ongoing maintenance such as hygiene appointments. Ask your dentist for a full breakdown before starting treatment.

mainEntity.name: How can I budget for dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start by booking a consultation to understand the full cost of your treatment plan. Ask about payment phasing and whether interest-free finance is available. Some practices also offer membership plans that reduce treatment costs. Having a detailed written estimate helps you plan with confidence.

mainEntity.name: Can I spread the cost of dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many practices offer finance options, including 0% interest plans, that allow you to spread the cost over several months. Eligibility usually depends on a credit check. Treatment costs may also be spread across the different stages of the implant process.
